issues.item: Triggers: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'people who look similar to the victims' is clinically incoherent because the patient is the victim; a plausible trigger would be people resembling the perpetrator(s) or contextual robbery cues. As written, this item conflicts with the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling dirty/contaminated is not impossible after robbery, but in this profile it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the selected items, which otherwise center on danger, self-blame, and moral injury rather than sexual violation or disgust-based trauma themes. This makes the appraisal set clinically inconsistent with the trauma context.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'Being naked' as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless there was a stripping/sexual humiliation element, which is not suggested elsewhere in the profile. The other trigger items point to perpetrator proximity and assault cues, making this vulnerability trigger clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' implies morally troubling behaviour during the event, but the rest of the profile reflects victim-focused danger, self-blame, and mistrust rather than any specific morally injurious action. In a mugging/robbery context this item is difficult to justify without corroborating memory/appraisal content about the patient's own behaviour.

vignette:
Malia, a 35-year-old accountant living in Honolulu with her husband, was walking home from the bus stop one evening when a man came up behind her, grabbed her shoulder, and yanked her purse strap. She turned and saw his face—young, angry, inches from hers—as he shoved her hard against a wall. Her lip split against her teeth, and she tasted blood, sharp and metallic, for hours afterward. He ran off with her bag. The whole thing lasted maybe ten seconds, but it reshaped everything.

In the weeks that followed, Malia found herself unable to stop replaying the moment. She would lie awake at night going over what she could have done differently: walked on the other side of the street, carried her bag across her body instead of loosely over one shoulder, left work earlier. She ruminated endlessly on how it might have been prevented, and each time she landed on a new detail she should have changed, she felt a fresh wave of guilt. It was her fault. The event happened because of the sort of person she was—careless, trusting, too slow to react. The world now felt permanently dangerous, a place where any ordinary street corner could become a trap. Her memory of the mugging was oddly vivid yet detached. When a sudden smell or sound brought it back, she could taste that metallic blood on her tongue again, as if it were fresh. At the same time, her body would lock into the exact position she had been in when the man grabbed her—shoulders hunched, arms pinned, back against the wall—and she would feel frozen, unable to move or speak. The memory felt so extreme that sometimes she had to remind herself it was real; it was hard to believe it had actually happened to her.

Then came the first time she saw someone who looked like him. About a month after the mugging, Malia was at a grocery store picking up ingredients for dinner. She rounded an aisle and a young man with the same wiry build, the same dark hoodie, reached for a box of cereal. Her chest seized. The metallic taste flooded her mouth, and for a second she was back against that wall, unable to breathe. She dropped her basket and fled the store, leaving her cart in the middle of the aisle. After that, she began scanning every face she passed—walking into her office building, waiting for coffee, driving through a parking lot. Each time she spotted a man with a similar jawline or a certain shade of dark hair, her pulse would spike and she would cross the street or duck into a shop. She had come to believe that the offender could be anywhere, that his face was generic enough to be hiding in plain sight. At work, she found herself constantly listening for footsteps in the hallway behind her desk. If she heard them approaching, her heart would race and she would angle her chair so no one could come up from behind. Two months ago, a colleague tapped her shoulder to ask a question, and she screamed in front of the whole office. After that, she started working with her back to the wall, facing the door.

Malia developed small but powerful strategies to cope. Whenever a memory surfaced, she would deliberately try to leave her body or blank out, focusing on a spot on the ceiling until the room felt distant and muffled. Her husband told her repeatedly that she was safe, that the mugger was caught and in jail, but Malia could not believe it. Even when she was at home with the doors locked, she could not truly relax. She stayed vigilant, her shoulders tight, scanning for signs of threat. At work, if a spreadsheet took longer to reconcile than expected, her mind would immediately jump to catastrophe—something bad must be happening, someone must be coming for her. Deadlines became a source of dread. Her avoidance spread. She stopped leaving the office after dark, even though it meant rushing through her closing tasks. She no longer walked to the bus stop; she made her husband pick her up every evening, a routine that strained their evenings and left her feeling dependent and ashamed. She stopped going to grocery stores alone, stopped jogging in the neighborhood park. Her world shrank. But the most insidious avoidance was the way she now navigated every public space—eyes darting, checking every male face, ready to retreat if the wrong features appeared.

What finally brought Malia to seek help was a panic attack in a client meeting. She had been asked to present a quarterly report, but when a manager asked a follow-up question and paused too long before responding, she felt her chest tighten, tasted blood in her mouth, and had to excuse herself to the restroom, where she sat on the floor dissociating for fifteen minutes. Her husband found her there. That night he told her gently that something had to change. Malia is terrified that she will never feel safe again, but she is also desperate to stop living inside fear—to return to herself, to her work, to a life that does not revolve around what happened in those ten seconds and the face that still haunts her in every crowd. She wants to believe it is possible, but she is not sure she does yet.
